name: AWS Lake Formation
oneLiner: Central permissions and governance layer over an S3 data lake.
whatItIs: Lake Formation sits on top of S3 and the Glue Data Catalog to add centralised security and governance to a data lake. Instead of managing a tangle of S3 bucket policies and IAM rules, you grant database/table/column/row permissions in one place, and services like Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue enforce them. It also helps build the lake — blueprints to ingest data, plus tag-based access control (LF-Tags) to manage permissions at scale. The point is one governance model for who can see which data in the lake, expressed in familiar table terms rather than raw storage ACLs.

inPractice.narrative: An org has a shared S3 data lake catalogued in Glue, used by many teams via Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Rather than hand-crafting bucket policies, an admin uses Lake Formation to grant the finance team SELECT on certain tables, mask a PII column from analysts, and restrict a region's rows to that region's team — all with LF-Tags. When anyone queries via Athena, Lake Formation enforces exactly those grants. It's the permission brain over the lake the query engines obey.

coreConcepts.detail: Grant access at database, table, column and row level (plus cell masking) in catalog terms — far more granular and manageable than S3/IAM policies.
Attach tags to catalog resources and grant permissions on tags, so access scales by policy instead of enumerating every table — the key to governing a large lake.
Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue honour Lake Formation grants at query time, giving consistent security across tools.
Workflows to ingest data from databases/logs into the lake and register it in the catalog, bootstrapping the lake.
Lake Formation registers S3 locations and vends temporary credentials to query engines, so users don't need direct bucket access.
Share catalog resources securely across AWS accounts (often with Resource Access Manager) for data-mesh-style setups.

whenToUse: Centralising fine-grained access control over an S3 + Glue data lake.
Column/row-level security and PII masking across query engines.
Managing permissions at scale with tag-based policies (LF-Tags).
Sharing governed lake data across teams or AWS accounts.
Replacing brittle hand-managed S3/IAM policies for analytics data.
whenNotToUse: A small single-team lake where basic IAM/bucket policies are enough.
Non-AWS-native query tools that don't integrate with Lake Formation enforcement.
Governing data outside the S3/Glue catalog world — it's lake-scoped.
Operational database access control — that's IAM/DB-native, not Lake Formation.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Central security/governance layer over S3 + Glue Catalog.

keyFacts.label: Granularity
keyFacts.value: Database, table, column, row, cell masking.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: No separate charge for LF itself; pay for underlying S3/Glue/query services.

pricingShape: Lake Formation itself is essentially free to use — there's no per-permission or per-governance charge for its core access control. You pay for the services underneath: S3 storage and requests, the Glue Data Catalog and crawlers, and the query engines (Athena scan cost, Redshift, EMR). So governance doesn't add a compute bill; it adds a control plane. The value is operational — replacing sprawling IAM/bucket policies with manageable, auditable grants — rather than a cost trade-off.
gotchas: Adopting it changes the permission model — mixing legacy IAM/bucket policies with LF grants causes confusing access failures; migrate deliberately.
Only integrated engines enforce LF permissions; a tool with raw S3 access can bypass them, so lock down direct bucket access.
LF-Tag design needs planning up front — ad-hoc tags become as messy as the policies you replaced.
Row-level/cell filtering has engine-specific support and limits — verify your query engine honours the feature you need.
Cross-account sharing setup (RAM, resource links) is fiddly and easy to misconfigure.
